title: Going to the baths
hook: before going out, picture what happens at the public baths: splashing, shoving, theft, and keep your purpose (Enchiridion 4)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Epictetus and the jug, naming what you love for what it is. Your line was clay breaks; that's part of what clay is. Today rounds off year two's first week.
screen: `CLAY BREAKS; THAT'S PART OF WHAT CLAY IS.`

segments.voice: A public bathhouse, a busy afternoon. Steam, echoing tile, a hundred voices. Somebody cannonballs into the pool and soaks your towel. Somebody shoves past you on the wet steps. Somebody shouts insults across the room. And somebody, while you're in the water, walks off with your sandals. None of it is strange for a crowded bath; it is simply what happens there. This is the scene Epictetus chooses for section four: not a battlefield, an afternoon errand. Today: going to the baths.
screen: `STEAM, TILE, A HUNDRED VOICES.` → `SPLASHED, SHOVED, ROBBED.` → `GOING TO THE BATHS.`

segments.voice: When you're about to do anything, Epictetus says, remind yourself what kind of activity it is. If you're going out to bathe, picture what happens at the baths: people who splash you, push, insult you, steal. Nothing mysterious; just honest weather for that place. Having pictured it, say to yourself: I want to bathe, and to keep my purpose in line with nature. Notice the and. You're going for a bath, and to stay the kind of person you mean to be while you're there. Then, he says, if something gets in the way of your bath, you'll have the words ready: I didn't want only to bathe, but also to keep my purpose, and I won't keep it if I'm furious about every splash. The bath can go badly and the trip can still succeed, because half of what you came for was always yours. Today's bathhouse might be the grocery store at six, the family dinner where a certain uncle will say a certain thing, the group chat, the morning commute. None of it is a surprise, and yet it can still ambush you, because you walk in expecting only the errand. A one-minute preview at the door, and an and attached to the errand, changes what counts as a good outing. And a look back at the week: year two opened with a book for the hand, then two piles, then desire held lightly, a jug, and today the baths. Each one is small enough to carry out the door.
screen: `PICTURE WHAT HAPPENS THERE.` · `I WANT TO BATHE, AND KEEP MY PURPOSE.` · `THE BATH FAILS, THE TRIP SUCCEEDS.` · `TODAY'S BATHHOUSE.` · then, large: `AND KEEP MY PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Walk through one outing ahead of you, a store, an office, a visit, a phone call, and let the usual snags appear without bracing: the line, the delay, the comment, the noise. Then say your sentence inside: I want to do this errand, and keep my purpose. Picture yourself in the middle of the worst moment, still steady.
Epictetus, previewing an errand: picture what usually happens, then go with two aims, the errand and your own purpose. Today's word.
Your line: and keep my purpose. The errand, and the purpose: two aims at every door. A week of year two, complete.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners take a moment before an outing to picture its usual frustrations and name their aim: to do the errand and stay the person they mean to be.

trapdoor: what you thought: expect the worst so you're not disappointed.
what it means: picture what the place is usually like, then go with two aims, the errand and your purpose.
what a scholar hears: 'in line with nature' (kata phusin) is the Stoic phrase; the purpose is prohairesis, the will, the one thing Epictetus calls truly ours.

Epictetus.meaning: a Stoic teacher who grew up enslaved and wrote nothing himself

bathhouse.meaning: a public bath, a crowded everyday place in the ancient world

in line with nature.meaning: the Stoic phrase for acting in agreement with nature and reason

purpose.meaning: your will or chosen aim, which Epictetus calls truly yours

notes: Review (2026-10-01): hook opened with the banned 'Picture'; removed the unsourced claim about bathhouse theft and curse tablets (and its myth item and source); softened 'ambushes us every time'.
